name: Malta
summary: A Mediterranean island nation, ruled by the Knights of St John (1530–1798) and Britain, independent since 1964.

knownFor.label: Megalithic temples
knownFor.note: Among the oldest free-standing buildings (about 3600 BCE).

knownFor.label: George Cross
knownFor.note: Awarded to the island in 1942 for courage in the Second World War.

knownFor.label: Valletta
knownFor.note: Fortified capital built by the Knights.

location.value: Three inhabited islands (Malta, Gozo, Comino) in the central Mediterranean, 93 km south of Sicily; about 316 km², the smallest EU country.

terrain.value: Low limestone hills and cliffs, with natural harbours such as Valletta’s Grand Harbour; no rivers or lakes.

climate.value: Hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters; very little fresh water, so most drinking water comes from desalination.

resources.value: Few natural resources apart from limestone and sea salt; its deep harbours made it a prize for every Mediterranean power.

disasters.value: No major natural disasters in modern times; droughts and water shortage are the main environmental problems.

population.value: About 560,000, making it one of the most densely populated countries in the world.

urbanisation.value: Almost entirely urban; towns around the Grand Harbour merge into one built-up area. Valletta itself has only about 6,000 residents.

disease.value: Life expectancy over 82 years and a free public health service.

economicBase.value: Tourism, online gaming, financial services, shipping and ship registration, and a growing pharmaceutical sector.

tradeRoutes.value: On the main east–west Mediterranean shipping lane; Malta Freeport is a big container hub. EU member since 2004.

wealth.value: A high-income economy that grew fast after joining the EU.

moneyAndTax.value: The Maltese lira until the euro arrived in 2008; low effective company taxes attracted foreign firms.

inequality.value: Fairly low inequality, though housing costs have risen sharply.

governmentType.value: A parliamentary republic since 1974; the British monarch was head of state from 1964 to 1974.

keyRulers.value: Dom Mintoff (Labour, closed the British bases in 1979); Eddie Fenech Adami (took Malta into the EU).

succession.value: Elections every five years using the single transferable vote; politics is dominated by Labour and the Nationalist Party.

institutions.value: House of Representatives, an elected president with mainly ceremonial powers, and courts based on mixed civil and common law.

stability.value: Heavily bombed in the Second World War; the whole island was awarded the George Cross (1942).

eliteConflict.value: Fierce rivalry between Labour and the Nationalists; the murder of journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia (2017) led to a government crisis.

armyAndTech.value: Small Armed Forces of Malta, mostly maritime patrol; neutrality is written into the constitution.

majorWars.value: Great Siege by the Ottomans (1565); siege by Germany and Italy (1940–42).

alliancesRivals.value: EU member, neutral and not in NATO; hosted the 1989 Bush–Gorbachev summit.

inventions.value: No major inventions; known for its skilled shipbuilding and dockyards.

scienceEducation.value: University of Malta (roots in 1592); free education up to university.

openness.value: Very open, trading and tourist economy.

communicationTransport.value: Buses, ferries between Malta and Gozo, and an international airport; no railway since 1931.

religion.value: Catholic Christianity is the state religion; Malta was the last EU country to legalise divorce (2011).

languageWriting.value: Maltese, the only Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet and an official EU language, and English.

artsArchitecture.value: Megalithic temples (Ġgantija, about 3600 BCE) older than the pyramids, and Baroque Valletta built by the Knights of St John.

socialStructure.value: A prosperous society with strong family ties and a large foreign workforce.

sharedIdentity.value: Maltese language, Catholic faith and village festas.

dailyLife.value: Limestone houses and flats; pastizzi (pastry), rabbit stew, the evening passeggiata.

neighbours.value: Italy (Sicily) to the north, Libya and Tunisia to the south.

ideasReligions.value: Mixed Arab, Italian and British influences in language and customs.

colonisation.value: Ruled by Arabs, Normans, the Knights of St John (1530–1798), France (1798–1800) and Britain (1800–1964).

riseSignals.value: Independence from Britain (1964); British bases closed (1979).

peakPeriod.value: Fast growth after EU membership (2004) and the euro (2008).

declineSignals.value: No general decline; concerns over corruption and overbuilding.
